summary: Specifies a stable naming scheme for the nameservers that serve the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones, which hold data for reverse mapping from address to name. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: The phone book that goes from number to name is run by servers, and this gives those servers steady, easy-to-remember names.

subtitle: Stable, dedicated names for the servers that answer reverse DNS lookups for IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: The IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA zones, which map addresses back to names, were served by servers named in other, unrelated domains, so there was no stable naming scheme for them.
tldr.mechanism: Each zone gets its own dedicated set of nameserver names under IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA and IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, with the zones delegated to the same servers and glue records added to the ARPA zone.
tldr.outcome: IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA can use two separate sets of servers, names compress well in DNS messages, and IPv6 reverse lookups need fewer queries.

facts.label: Later name under the same domain

today: RFC 5855 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 155). The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The server lists and sizes in its appendices describe the situation at the time of writing in May 2010.

sections.title: Reverse Lookups and the ARPA Zones
sections.content:
The DNS supports keyed lookup using three namespaces: domain names, IPv4 addresses and IPv6 addresses. Mapping an IPv4 address to a name uses data in the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone, and IPv6 uses the IP6.ARPA zone. This address-to-name mapping is called a reverse lookup, and the zones support the reverse DNS.

The RFC calls the secure and stable hosting of these zones critical, since many applications rely on timely reverse lookup answers. When it was written, IN-ADDR.ARPA was served by a subset of the DNS root servers, and IP6.ARPA by servers operated by APNIC, ARIN, ICANN, LACNIC and the RIPE NCC. This document specifies a dedicated, stable set of nameserver names for each zone.
sections.eli5: Looking up a name from a number is like finding who owns a phone number. This RFC is about giving the helpers who answer that question proper, stable names.

sections.title: The IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA Names
sections.content:
Servers for IN-ADDR.ARPA are named A.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, B.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA and so on through F and beyond. The IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA zone is delegated to the same servers as IN-ADDR.ARPA, with IPv4 and IPv6 glue records for each server added to the ARPA zone.

Both zones share servers because they are dedicated to a single purpose and can reasonably share fate. All servers sit under one domain so that names compress well. Because glue exists in the ARPA zone for every server, using one domain is not a practical single point of failure.
sections.eli5: The helpers for the IPv4 phone book are named A, B, C and so on, all under one family name. That makes them easy to list.

sections.title: The IP6-SERVERS.ARPA Names and Separation
sections.content:
IP6.ARPA gets the same treatment: A.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA, B.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA and so on. The IP6-SERVERS.ARPA zone is delegated to the same servers as IP6.ARPA, and IPv4 and IPv6 glue records are added to the ARPA zone.

The scheme allows the two reverse zones to be delegated to two different sets of nameservers. That operational separation could keep a failure of the IN-ADDR.ARPA servers from hurting IPv6 reverse lookups as collateral damage. Choosing the operators of individual servers is out of scope; it is an IANA function under Section 4 of the MoU between the IETF and ICANN.
sections.eli5: The IPv6 phone book gets its own set of helpers with their own names, so if one set has a bad day the other keeps working.

sections.title: Performance: Compression and Query Counts
sections.content:
Appendix B argues the names are highly compressible. A full domain name encoding uses a one-byte length plus one byte per character for each label, and a terminating zero byte. Once one name is encoded, later names under the same domain need only their first label plus a two-byte pointer, which is 4 bytes. The first name, A.IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA, takes 24 bytes and A.IP6-SERVERS.ARPA takes 19.

For a twelve-record IN-ADDR.ARPA set the total is 68 bytes. For a six-record IP6.ARPA set it is 39 bytes, against 74 bytes for the existing IP6.ARPA set shown in Appendix A.

The appendix also walks through query patterns with an empty cache. With the old IP6.ARPA servers, the referral carries no glue, so a recursive lookup is needed to find a server address, and three queries are required in all cases. With the new names, the referral comes with glue, so no recursive lookup is needed.
sections.eli5: Names that share a family name can be written in a short way after the first one. That makes messages smaller and lookups quicker.

sections.title: What IANA Did and the IAB Statement
sections.content:
In its role of giving technical guidance to ICANN on the ARPA top-level domain (see RFC 3172), the IAB reviewed the proposal and supports it as an operational change in line with the roles of ICANN and the IAB.

IANA has delegated IN-ADDR-SERVERS.ARPA to the nameservers listed in Section 2 and IP6-SERVERS.ARPA to those in Section 3, and installed IPv4 and IPv6 glue records for those nameservers in the ARPA zone. The RFC says the new scheme introduces no additional security risks.
sections.eli5: The group that looks after the internet's address books said yes, and the record keeper set up the new names.
